edges.description: Recurrent alveolar hemorrhage and intra-alveolar hemosiderin accumulation drive type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and progressive fibrotic lung remodeling.
Bleeding into the alveolar spaces leads to expectoration of blood (hemoptysis).
Chronic sequestration of iron as hemosiderin within alveolar macrophages and recurrent alveolar blood loss deplete systemic iron stores, causing iron-deficiency anemia.
Alveolar filling with blood and resulting anemia impair gas exchange and oxygen delivery, producing dyspnea.
Alveolar filling with blood and hemosiderin-laden macrophages produces bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities and patchy infiltrates on chest imaging.
Chronic recurrent alveolar hemorrhage and parenchymal remodeling progress to interstitial pulmonary fibrosis if untreated.

nodes.description: Extravasation of red blood cells and hemoglobin into the alveolar space causes diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Alveolar macrophages phagocytose the extravasated erythrocytes and degrade hemoglobin into hemosiderin. These hemosiderin-laden macrophages (siderophages) accumulate in alveolar spaces and are detected via bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or lung biopsy as the hallmark histologic finding of alveolar bleeding.

nodes.description: Elimination of gluten from diet is foundational therapy for Lane Hamilton Syndrome, as it addresses the underlying celiac disease trigger. Many LHS cases achieve remission or significant improvement with strict, lifelong gluten-free diet adherence. Relapse commonly occurs with dietary nonadherence, emphasizing the critical importance of sustained dietary compliance for disease control.

evidence.snippet: The primary treatment for LHS is a GFD, which leads to the regression of both IPH and CD -related symptoms in most cases (4,9). While some patients may be prescribed steroids or other immunosuppressive drugs to control hemoptysis, GFD can lead to the discontinuation of these drugs in most patients.

nodes.description: Lane Hamilton Syndrome begins with celiac disease, an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically predisposed individuals. Gluten exposure activates intestinal immune responses with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia in the small intestine, particularly the duodenum. This localized intestinal autoimmunity generates systemic immune activation and circulating autoantibodies, including anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies.

nodes.description: Chronic recurrent alveolar hemorrhage and intra-alveolar hemosiderin accumulation are accompanied by reactive type II pneumocyte hyperplasia along the alveolar epithelium and mild-to-moderate interstitial fibrosis. If the underlying gluten-driven condition is not recognized and treated, repeated hemorrhagic episodes progress to worsening pulmonary hemosiderosis, interstitial fibrosis, and end-stage lung disease.
